title: Iran Struck Two US Bases — Then Took the SCO Podium to Offer a Deal
subtitle: Neither the US nor China appeared in the coverage of a US-Iran diplomatic signal. The two principal parties to the conflict were absent.
body_md:
The sequence of events mattered. US forces struck Iran's Larak Island on August 30 — the first military exchange in a month. Iran responded with ballistic missile strikes at two US air bases in Jordan. The following day, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian took the podium at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek and offered Washington a deal: "If the United States returns to its commitments under the aforementioned memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately take reciprocal action," as [Middle East Eye](https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/live-blog-update/pezeshkian-says-tehran-would-immediately-reciprocate-if-us-honours-june) reported.

The strategic positioning was intentional: strike, then offer terms. Iran arrived at a multilateral forum as the aggrieved party willing to negotiate, placing responsibility for de-escalation on Washington. [Globe and Mail](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/article-iran-us-war-trump-threatens-strikes/) captured the tension: "While neither side appears to want a return to all-out war, their pledges to respond to further attacks highlight how quickly a conflict that has increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action."

The MoU that Pezeshkian referenced — the June interim deal — collapsed, with both sides accusing each other of violating its terms. [The Hindu Intl](https://www.thehindu.com/news/international/iran-would-immediately-reciprocate-if-us-returns-to-june-deal-president-pezeshkian/article71414808.ece) was the only outlet to itemize Iran's full list of demands for reopening the Strait of Hormuz: lifting the naval blockade on Iranian ports, removing oil sanctions, and unfreezing Iranian assets abroad. That conditions list has not changed since the June deal collapsed. Pezeshkian's offer is conditional on US compliance with a set of demands Washington has not met.

Each outlet placed a different element at the center of the same event. [TASS English](https://tass.com/world/2180375) called the deal the "Islamabad Memorandum" — a label no other outlet in the corpus used — and described Iran's strikes as "proportionate," signaling Russian validation of Tehran's military conduct. [Tehran Times](https://www.tehrantimes.com/news/529560/SCO-summit-Iran-s-opportunity-to-contain-unilateralism) framed the SCO summit as Iran's "opportunity to contain unilateralism," elevating a bilateral ceasefire appeal into a multilateral power-balancing argument against the US. [Daily Sabah](https://www.dailysabah.com/world/mid-east/tehran-claims-ready-to-reciprocate-us-return-to-interim-peace-deal) applied skeptical language — "Tehran claims ready to reciprocate" — placing AKP-aligned Turkey at arm's length from Iran's offer despite shared Islamic-conservative orientation.

[Globe and Mail](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/article-iran-us-war-trump-threatens-strikes/) was the only outlet to report tankers "coming under fire leaving the Strait of Hormuz" — the most concrete detail in the corpus about what the Hormuz closure means for active commercial shipping right now. [Straits Times](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/middle-east/iran-urges-us-to-comply-with-interim-deal-after-trump-threatens-further-strikes) added domestic context: Iran's "plunging currency and high inflation" — the home-front economic pressure that explains why Tehran may need a deal despite its hardline posture and its military strikes.

The most significant gap in the corpus is structural. No US outlet appears, despite the story being a direct public diplomatic signal from Tehran to Washington. US press appears to have led with Trump's Fox News threat rather than Iran's conditional offer — meaning the US public largely didn't see the signal Iran was sending in Bishkek. No Chinese outlet appears either, despite China being a central SCO member physically present at the summit and a key economic partner to Iran. No UK outlet appears.

Three of the four most consequential external voices on the conflict's trajectory — the United States, China, and the UK — are absent from the day's recorded coverage of Iran's public diplomatic move. What the global press covered and what the three principal actors actually reported to their own publics are different stories.
